chief_complaint: sudden dyspnea, hypoxia, low BP after international flight
hpi_details: A 62-year-old female presents to the clinic with sudden dyspnea, hypoxia, low bp after international flight. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks the recirculated air on the plane gave her sudden severe pneumonia or that the exhaustion of the flight triggered a heart attack.
concerns: She is terrified that she is having a fatal heart attack and will pass away before seeing the grandchildren she flew across the world to visit.
expectations: She hopes to receive oxygen and have her heart checked so she can breathe comfortably and leave to stay with her family.

investigation_events.title: Bedside echocardiogram
investigation_events.availability_message: The bedside echocardiogram result is now available.

results.value: Severely dilated right ventricle with RV/LV ratio 1.4, interventricular septal flattening, and reduced right-ventricular free-wall motion; no pericardial effusion

clinical_knowledge.topic: Massive Pulmonary Embolism evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Massive Pulmonary Embolism is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Hypotension with suspected pulmonary embolism requires immediate resuscitation and urgent reperfusion-team assessment; bedside echocardiography or CT pulmonary angiography is chosen according to stability, and systemic thrombolysis or catheter/surgical reperfusion is considered promptly when no contraindication exists.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden dyspnea, hypoxia, low BP after international flight

Key HPI features: A 62-year-old female presents to the clinic with sudden dyspnea, hypoxia, low bp after international flight. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Massive Pulmonary Embolism.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Massive Pulmonary Embolism.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Myocardial infarction without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Hypotension with hypoxia.
management_principles: Resuscitate immediately, obtain bedside echocardiography or CT pulmonary angiography according to stability, start anticoagulation when appropriate, and obtain urgent reperfusion-team assessment for thrombolysis or catheter/surgical reperfusion
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: A large clot in the pulmonary arteries causing sudden breathlessness and low blood pressure after a long flight.

must_ask.say: Did you have a long flight recently?
Does it hurt more when you breathe?

history.answer: I suddenly became terribly short of breath right after getting off an international flight, and I feel so weak and faint.
It started suddenly about two hours ago right after our flight landed, and it has been getting worse ever since.
I am struggling to breathe even while sitting completely still, and any small movement makes me gasp for air.
It has been persistent and steadily worsening since it began, and I have never experienced anything like this before.
Lying flat makes me feel like I am suffocating even more, but this just started a couple of hours ago so I haven't tried to sleep.
Any slight movement or taking a deep breath makes it worse, and resting has not helped at all.
No, I haven't noticed any whistling or wheezing noises when I breathe.
I have a dry, hacking cough that started with this shortness of breath, but no phlegm and no fever or chills.
I have a sharp, stabbing pain on the right side of my chest that gets much worse whenever I try to take a breath.
My heart is pounding very fast, and I felt intensely lightheaded and almost blacked out when I stood up at baggage claim.
No, I haven't coughed up any blood or pink-tinged mucus.
No, I haven't had swelling in both legs or any sudden weight gain recently.

history.answer: My right calf felt swollen, tight, and crampy yesterday during our fourteen-hour flight from Europe, where I remained seated almost the entire time.

history.answer: I feel completely exhausted and drained, but I have not had pale skin, black tarry stools, or any unusual bleeding.
I feel very frightened and anxious because I cannot catch my breath, but I have no tingling or numbness around my lips or hands.
No, I have never had heart attacks, heart failure, asthma, or COPD, and I don't use any inhalers.
No, I worked in an office as an accountant and have never been exposed to industrial dust, asbestos, birds, or mold.
I am not taking any blood pressure pills, painkillers, chemotherapy, or heart rhythm medicines like amiodarone.
No, I went through menopause over ten years ago and have never taken hormone replacement therapy or birth control pills.

I thought maybe I picked up a bad lung infection from the airplane air, or the long flight put too much strain on my heart. I'm terrified that my heart is giving out and I won't even get to see my grandchildren after traveling all this way.
I have always been healthy with no high blood pressure, diabetes, or other chronic conditions.
I have never had any surgeries, major injuries, or hospital stays.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or vitamins.
I have no known allergies to any medications or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products.
I only drink an occasional glass of wine at social gatherings, once or twice a month at most.
I am a retired accountant and live at home with my husband.
There is no family history of blood clots, pulmonary embolism, heart problems, or early deaths.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 84/52 mmHg, pulse 118 beats/min, respiratory rate 26 breaths/min, temperature 36.6 °C, and oxygen saturation 86% on room air.
Patient appears acutely distressed, tachypneic, diaphoretic, using accessory neck muscles to breathe, with mild peripheral cyanosis and no digital clubbing.
Jugular venous distension present at 6 cm above the sternal angle at a 45-degree angle.
Symmetric chest expansion with no chest wall tenderness or subcutaneous emphysema.
Resonant percussion notes throughout all lung fields bilaterally.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally in all lung zones with no wheezing, rhonchi, or crackles.
Rapid regular rhythm with an accentuated pulmonic component of the second heart sound (loud P2); no murmurs or third heart sound.
Radial and dorsalis pedis pulses are rapid, thready, and weak bilaterally, with cool distal extremities.
No bilateral dependent pitting edema; swelling is isolated to the right lower leg.
Right calf is warm, erythematous, swollen with a 3 cm larger circumference than the left, and distinctly tender to palpation.
